body.heading: Falling, but slowly
paragraphs: A falling body speeds up until the air resistance pushing against it balances gravity, then falls at a steady terminal velocity. For a skydiver falling flat, that is about 200 kilometres per hour — far too fast to survive landing.

A parachute changes the balance by catching the air. Its canopy presents a huge area to the airflow and traps a mass of air beneath it, producing enormous drag. With far more resistance at far lower speed, the new terminal velocity is only about 20 kilometres per hour.

body.heading: The canopy at work
paragraphs: Modern sport parachutes are not umbrellas but inflatable wings — ram-air canopies with cells that fill with air and hold an aerofoil shape. The jumper steers by pulling toggles that deform one side, and flares the wing before landing to slow the descent further.

Round canopies, still used for cargo and some military drops, work as pure drag devices: they spill a little air through a vent at the top to stop the canopy rocking like a pendulum as it descends. The steadiness matters in itself: a swinging load lands badly, so a calm descent is a safety feature, not a luxury.

body.heading: A landing like jumping off a wall
paragraphs: At about five metres per second, touching down under a parachute is like jumping from a wall a little over a metre high — firm, but easily absorbed by bent legs. Compare the unbraked fall: hitting the ground at 200 kilometres per hour is unsurvivable.

The same drag principle, scaled up, lands spacecraft: capsules returning from orbit deploy parachutes to shed their last few hundred kilometres per hour, splashing down or touching desert at speeds a crew can walk away from.

description: A parachute trades speed for drag: its wide canopy catches so much air that a lethal fall becomes a gentle landing.
